subject: [PATCH 2/2] x86/kstack_erase: Use REP STOSQ for large stack fills

reviews.author: Nick Desaulniers
reviews.summary: The reviewer noted that REP STOSQ is used elsewhere in the kernel, specifically in memset64 of arch/x86/include/asm/string_64.h, and requested to consider consistency across all uses.
reviews.raw_body:
Surely this isn't the only place using `rep stosq` in the tree, right?
It's not, see memset64 in arch/x86/include/asm/string_64.h.

2026-11-19.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the stack erasure process on x86-64 architecture by using REP STOSQ instruction to fill large spans of memory, which is more efficient than the generic __stackleak_poison() function that uses a word loop. The patch introduces an inline assembly implementation for __stackleak_poison() on x86-64, which fills spans larger than 512 bytes with REP STOSQ and falls back to the word loop for shorter spans. This change reduces the overhead of stack erasure by up to 35% in certain scenarios, making it a performance improvement.

reviews.author: Peter Zijlstra
reviews.summary: Reviewer Peter Zijlstra questioned the REP STOSQ setup cost, suggesting that 16-32 words would be sufficient to amortize it, and proposed an unrolled loop for smaller counts, also recommending making memset64() __always_inline.

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the REP STOSQ instruction is not properly aligned for 64-bit accesses, which could lead to incorrect stack poisoning and requested the use of a different alignment.

Reviewer David Laight pointed out that recent GCC versions have issues optimizing the REP STOSQ loop, and suggested unrolling the loop 4 times for better performance on newer CPUs. However, he also noted that this approach may not work due to potential pipeline stalls.

Reviewer David Laight questioned the usefulness of the patch, noting that memset_p() and memset_l() have almost no users.

reviews.author: Peter Zijlstra
reviews.summary: Reviewer Peter Zijlstra suggested an optimization to the __stackleak_poison function, replacing the REP STOSQ instruction for large stack fills with a call to memset64 when the count is less than 32, to amortize the startup cost of REP STOSQ.

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight pointed out that the REP STOSQ instruction used in __stackleak_poison() may not be optimal for all CPU architectures, as it relies on the CPU's ability to execute a REP prefix followed by an STOSQ instruction. He suggested considering alternative instructions or approaches that are more portable across different CPUs.

Reviewer David Laight pointed out that the addition of `erase_low += 32` should be placed within a specific section of code, likely to adjust the loop counter for REP STOSQ instruction

Reviewer David Laight noted that the REP STOSQ instruction may not be optimal for CPUs that can perform two writes per clock cycle, suggesting a loop that uses two movq instructions to write 32 bytes at a time would be more efficient. He also provided an example of how this could be achieved using OPTIMIZER_HIDE_VAR() and demonstrated the generated assembly code on godbolt.org.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:38:25 +0000
David Laight <david.laight.linux@gmail.com> wrote:

---

The add (probably) needs to be in the middle...
 			erase_low += 32;

---

I threw in enough OPTIMIZER_HIDE_VAR() to stop the optimiser breaking
the code. https://godbolt.org/z/nx477T4M1
gcc then generates:
        movq    %rdx, (%rdi)
        movq    %rdx, 8(%rdi)
        addq    $32, %rdi
        movq    %rdx, -16(%rdi)
        movq    %rdx, -8(%rdi)
.L32:
        subq    $4, %rcx
        jns     .L22
for the code loop (clang is a bit worse - but should be ok).
I think that will be a 'two clock loop' on cpu that can do
two writes/clock; zen3 and ice lake).
For 'stack splatting' rounding up to a multiple of 32 bytes
will save all the 'remainder' code.

David

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight pointed out that the REP STOSQ instruction is not properly aligned for 64-bit accesses, which could lead to a data corruption issue.

Reviewer David Laight expressed skepticism about the performance benefits of using REP STOSQ for large stack fills, suggesting that it may not be effective across all CPU architectures.

The reviewer, David Laight, expressed strong disagreement with the patch's inline assembly code, citing performance concerns and suggesting optimizations to reduce instruction count, loop control code, and register dependency chain length. He also asked if the length of the stores can be a multiple of 32 and noted that REP STOS might be faster when the destination is 64-byte aligned.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 20 Nov 2026 11:45:34 +0100
Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org> wrote:

---

That really does sound like wishful thinking.
Especially if you go back a few generations on the cpu architecture.

---

That looks horrid to me.
You want as few instructions (especially conditionals) inside the
loop as possible.
The Intel cpu will execute a two clock loop and the later ones will
do two writes per clock
(zen5 will execute a one clock loop and do two writes/clock).
So you want a loop with just 4 writes and the loop control code.
The 'pointer add' just needs to execute at the same time as some
of the stores - to avoid lengthening the register dependency chain.

For this code, can the length be a multiple of 32?
Also on some cpu the 'rep stos' might be twice as fast (per byte) if
the destination in 64 byte aligned - true for 'rep movsb'.

David

reviews.author: Peter Zijlstra
reviews.summary: Reviewer Peter Zijlstra questioned the relevance of optimizing for Interlagos, an older CPU model, and suggested that Nehalem and later CPUs should be sufficient to benefit from the REP STOSQ optimization.
reviews.raw_body:
How old? I mean, Interlagos old, sure, but nobody should care about
performance there I think.

AFAICT Nehalem and later should be good with the 16-32 words. As would
all the various Zen chips.

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight pointed out that the REP STOSQ instruction is not properly aligned for 64-bit accesses, which could lead to incorrect results or crashes.

Reviewer David Laight questioned the accuracy of the setup costs for REP STOSQ and REP MOVQ instructions on various architectures, citing a lack of reliable sources and potential issues with alignment and I-cache misses.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 20 Nov 2026 16:35:39 +0100
Peter Zijlstra <peterz@infradead.org> wrote:

---

Have you got an accurate source for the setup costs for 'rep stos/movs'
for the various architectures?
I didn't find one last time I looked.
Last time I measured rep movs I was using mfence to synchronise with rdpmc
and that takes even longer - so you only get the per-byte costs.
(You can use data-dependencies which have minimal overhead unless you
go back to to some pre-zen amd cpu.)

You get 16 bytes/clock until Haswell which will do 32 if rdi is aligned.
Icelake might increase that to 64 bytes/clock.
Agner has zen2 onwards at 32 bytes/clock.

Agner also has zen3 and Icelake being able to do 2 writes per clock.
If that is achievable for the writes being done (the loop isn't a
problem) then it also takes a while for the 'rep stos' to catch up.
(Then you have the cost of the I-cache misses ...)

David

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary: Author acknowledges that REP STOSQ does not provide a performance benefit for stackleak_erase() and prefers v2.1 over v2.2, but is willing to send v2.2 if reviewers strongly prefer it.

reviews.author: Usama Arif (author)
reviews.summary: The author addressed a concern about rounding up or down the erase_high value, explaining that it must be exact due to alignment requirements and potential corruption of live stack data or STACK_END_MAGIC.
reviews.raw_body:
The range can't be rounded: erase_low is wherever the poison search
stopped, and erase_high is the stack pointer or the bottom of pt_regs
(168 bytes, so only 8-byte aligned). Rounding up writes live stack,
rounding down can write STACK_END_MAGIC when the stack was used to the
end.

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the inline asm in __stackleak_poison() uses the 'c' constraint, which is not valid for REP STOSQ instructions, and requested a change to use the 'D' constraint instead.

Reviewer David Laight questioned the performance measurement and suggested using 'rep stos' for all lengths to avoid branch misprediction penalties, noting that it may still be beneficial even if slightly slower for short lengths.
reviews.raw_body:
On Thu, 19 Nov 2026 13:31:08 -0800
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

As a matter of interest (and separately from the exact code) how did you
measure the performance to get the 300-400 byte gain point?

If the count is variable - likely in real life, you'll get a branch
misprediction penalty (about 20 clocks on zen5) every time you change
between the two choices.
The copy loop will have another mispredict penalty for the loop itself.

So you are likely to get an overall improvement if you use 'rep stos'
for all lengths - even the ones for with it is slightly slower.
Unless, that is, you know at compile time that most of the length
will be short.

David

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the REP STOSQ instruction may not be optimal for all CPU architectures, and requested further investigation to ensure it is the best choice for x86-64.

Reviewer David Laight questioned the effectiveness of the code, pointing out that task_low_bound() could return an aligned address and suggesting rounding down the length to avoid leaving the last few words alone. He also wondered if STACK_END_MAGIC and STACK_ERASE_POISON need different values, given the presence of a guard page in modern stack allocation.
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:46:01 +0000
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

If the stack down by STACK_END_MAGIC has been written you are almost in
'deep do-do land' so task_low_bound() could return an aligned address
and that would let you align down the low address.
(So leaving the very last few words alone.)
It also probably doesn't really matter about the top few words.
So the length could be rounded down.

Alternatively, do STACK_END_MAGIC and STACK_ERASE_POISON even need
to have different values?
(And aren't stacks now allocated with a guard page - so you get a
fault on overflow much earlier than any check for STACK_END_MAGIC.)

But does this code even work in a useful manner.
It seems to stop scanning after finding 128 bytes of KSTACK_ERASE_POISON.
Isn't that going to stop on a function with a large on-stack buffer
(especially since one is likely to be on the deepest part of the stack).
I'd have thought you'd jump down the stack in larger lumps than that
just looking for an unwritten word before even trying to decide if it
was the boundary.

David

reviews.author: David Laight
reviews.summary:
Reviewer David Laight noted that the REP STOSQ instruction may not be optimal for all x86-64 CPUs, as it relies on the CPU's ability to execute REP instructions in a single clock cycle, which is not guaranteed across all CPUs.

Reviewer David Laight requested specific information about the lengths of stack erases and questioned the source of a performance metric, suggesting that the code loop and REP STOSQ instructions be timed separately.

Reviewer David Laight suggested an alternative implementation for the stackleak poison function, proposing to use a switch statement with Duff's device to reduce the number of conditions in the loop.

Reviewer David Laight noted that on Zen5, the REP STOSQ instruction can execute a loop in one clock cycle and suggested unrolling the loop only once to avoid unnecessary overhead, potentially improving performance.

Reviewer David Laight suggested testing the patch on older Intel CPUs, noting that the setup costs of REP STOSQ may be higher due to features like Fast Return from Interrupt (FRMS)
reviews.raw_body:
On Fri, 20 Nov 2026 18:43:38 +0000
Usama Arif <usama.arif@linux.dev> wrote:

---

What are the lengths of those erases?
(and where does the 46ns come from??)
I'd definitely time 'just the code loop  - various loops' and
'just rep stos'.

---

To many conditions in the loop.
You could do it this way:
	switch (count & 3) {
	case 0: do { *ptr++ = poison;
	case 3:      *ptr++ = poison;
	case 2:      *ptr++ = poison;
	case 1:      *ptr++ = poison;
		} while ((count -= 4) > 0);
	}
(give or take some off-by-one here and there).
But I suspect that using Duff's device is frowned up.

---

For zen5 you should only need to unroll the loop once (two writes per iteration).
In my experiments it can execute a loop in one clock.
Unless the compiler unrolled it for you (and got it right!) the original
loop would be half the speed

---

I'd also try some older Intel cpu.
The setup costs are likely to be higher with FRMS and friends.

David

The patch introduces an inline assembly implementation for __stackleak_poison() on x86-64, which fills spans larger than 512 bytes with REP STOSQ and falls back to the word loop for shorter spans. This change reduces the overhead of stack erasure by up to 35% in certain scenarios, making it a performance improvement.
